title: Daniel Cormier, Joe Rogan Slam “Ungrateful Loser” Gable Steveson After UFC 331 Knockout Loss
body:
The UFC heavyweight landscape was jolted on Saturday night when Gable Steveson, the 2021 Olympic gold‑medalist turned prospect, suffered a first‑round knockout at UFC 331. The loss not only ended his unbeaten streak but also ignited a wave of criticism from veteran voices in the sport. Former champion and current commentator Daniel Cormier, alongside longtime podcaster and UFC analyst Joe Rogan, publicly called out Steveson’s post‑fight demeanor, labeling him an “ungrateful loser” and warning that the young fighter still has much to learn about professionalism inside and outside the octagon.

Steveson entered the bout riding a wave of hype that positioned him as the next dominant force in the heavyweight division. After a flawless amateur career capped by Olympic gold, his transition to mixed martial arts was swift and impressive; a string of decisive victories against seasoned opponents suggested a meteoric rise. The hype, however, also brought scrutiny. Critics have long noted that his wrestling pedigree does not automatically translate to the striking and defensive nuances required at the elite UFC level. The knockout—delivered by a well‑timed left hook from his opponent—exposed gaps in his striking defense and raised questions about his readiness for the division’s top tier.

Cormier’s reaction was blunt. In a post‑fight interview, he praised Steveson’s athleticism but emphasized that talent alone does not secure longevity in the UFC. “He’s got the tools, no doubt,” Cormier said, “but you can’t walk into a fight, get knocked out, and then act like you’re entitled to the spotlight. The sport demands humility and a willingness to improve.” Rogan, echoing similar sentiments on his podcast, described Steveson’s on‑camera interview after the loss as “defensive and ungrateful,” suggesting the young heavyweight seemed more concerned with preserving his brand than acknowledging the defeat. Both veterans highlighted that the mental component of fighting—accepting loss, learning from it, and showing respect to opponents—remains as critical as physical preparation.

The criticism is not without precedent. The UFC has seen several highly touted prospects stumble when faced with early adversity. Fighters such as Francis Ngannou and Jon Jones have both endured setbacks that forced them to reassess training methods, coaching staff, and even personal attitudes. In Steveson’s case, the immediate fallout may involve a reevaluation of his coaching team’s approach to striking defense and fight IQ. Analysts point out that his reliance on wrestling, while a potent weapon, can become a liability if he fails to develop a credible stand‑up game capable of both delivering and absorbing blows.

Beyond the technical aspects, the incident underscores a broader cultural shift within mixed martial arts. Social media platforms have amplified athletes’ personas, often rewarding bravado over humility. Steveson’s post‑fight comments, which some interpreted as dismissive of his opponent’s skill, clash with the sport’s evolving expectations for sportsmanship. As the UFC continues to expand globally, its stars are increasingly expected to model professionalism that resonates with a diverse fan base. The backlash from Cormier and Rogan may serve as a cautionary tale for other rising fighters navigating the delicate balance between confidence and entitlement.

Looking ahead, Steveson’s next steps will be closely watched. A measured response—perhaps a candid apology, a commitment to refine his striking, and a renewed focus on respect for the competition—could rehabilitate his image and preserve his trajectory as a heavyweight contender. Conversely, a defensive stance might deepen the skepticism surrounding his readiness for the division’s elite. The UFC’s heavyweight division remains wide open, and the ability of a promising athlete like Steveson to adapt after a crushing defeat will not only define his own career but also influence how the organization cultivates and mentors its next generation of champions.
